title.en: Where does your own history begin?

text.en: Think of your earliest memory. How old were you, and who was there? Your memories, your photographs and the stories told by your family are all sources of your own past. Historians do the same thing for the whole of humanity, but over thousands of years. In this chapter we learn how historical time is measured, how sources help us, and how the earliest humans lived.

The Earth has a very long history of about 4.54 billion years, and humans occupy only a tiny, recent part of it. Several kinds of experts help us uncover the past. Geologists study the physical features of the Earth, such as soil, rocks, mountains and rivers. Palaeontologists study the remains of plants, animals and humans from millions of years ago in the form of fossils. A fossil is an impression or part of a plant or animal preserved in layers of soil or rock. Anthropologists study human societies and cultures from the oldest times to the present. Archaeologists dig up what people, plants and animals left behind, such as tools, pots, beads, toys, bones, burnt grains, parts of houses and bricks.
Every society has had its own way of measuring time. Big events, such as the birth of an important person or the start of a ruler reign, have often marked the beginning of a new era, which is a distinct period of time. Today the Gregorian calendar is used worldwide. It has 12 months adding up to 365 days, with a leap year every four years. Century years like 1800, 1900 and 2000 are leap years only if they are multiples of 400, so among those only 2000 is a leap year. Hindu, Muslim, Jewish, Chinese and other calendars are also used for festivals. The Gregorian calendar counts years from the conventional year of the birth of Jesus Christ. Years after it used to be marked AD, and are now called Common Era or CE. Years before it used to be marked BC and are now called Before Common Era or BCE. India gained independence in 1947 CE, and the Buddha was born about 560 BCE. There is no year zero. Year 1 CE comes right after year 1 BCE, so only 3 years pass between 2 BCE and 2 CE. To find the gap between a BCE date and a CE date, add them and subtract 1. Using that rule, if the year is 2024 CE, the Buddha was born 560 plus 2024 minus 1, which is 2583 years ago. A timeline is a handy tool that shows a sequence of dates and events. It helps us see the order of events: even without dates you can see that the birth of the Buddha came before that of Jesus. A decade is ten years. A century is 100 years, counted from year 1 CE, so we are in the 21st century, from 2001 to 2100. The 3rd century BCE covers 300 BCE to 201 BCE. A millennium is 1000 years, and we are in the 3rd millennium CE, from 2001 to 3000. Many Indian calendars depend on the positions of the Sun and the Moon. A panchanga is a book of tables listing the days of each month with astronomical data, such as eclipses and the times of sunrise and sunset. It also gives festival dates and often weather predictions.
A source of history is a place, person, text or object that gives information about a past event or period. Your family photos, diaries, ID cards and the memories of relatives are sources for your family history. Historians gather information from many kinds of sources: oral sources such as folklore and stories, literary sources such as the Vedas, Itihasas, poems, plays and historical texts, archaeological sources such as coins, tools, pottery and remains, and structures such as monuments and mounds. There are also artistic sources such as paintings and sculptures, inscriptions on copper plates, and accounts of foreign travellers. Like pieces of a jigsaw puzzle, sources may match or contradict one another. When they disagree, historians must decide which source to trust more. In history, some pieces of the puzzle may always stay missing. Many specialists help: historians, archaeologists, epigraphists who study ancient inscriptions, anthropologists, and experts in literature and languages. In the last 50 years science has added studies of ancient climates, chemical tests of excavated material and the genetics of ancient people. For recent history of the last two or three centuries, newspapers are another source, and for recent decades so are television and the internet.
Modern humans, Homo sapiens, have walked the Earth for about 300000 years, which is a tiny part of the history of the Earth. Early humans faced many challenges from nature and lived in groups to help one another. They looked constantly for shelter and food and were hunters and gatherers, which means they hunted animals and collected edible plants and fruits. They lived in temporary camps, rock shelters and caves, and spoke languages that are now lost. They used fire and made improved stone axes, blades and arrowheads. They also believed in natural forces and may have had an idea of an afterlife. Rock paintings in hundreds of caves all over the world show their lives. Some show simple figures or symbols, others show scenes with animals or people. They also made simple ornaments such as shell or stone beads and pendants of animal teeth, and traded them with other groups.
The climate of the Earth has changed many times. During an Ice Age, much of the Earth was covered with ice. The last Ice Age lasted from over 100000 years ago to about 12000 years ago. When the climate warmed, the ice partly melted and the water swelled rivers and flowed into the oceans. Living conditions improved and in many parts of the world people began to settle and grow cereals and grains. They also tamed animals such as cattle and goats. With more food, communities grew in size and number and settled near rivers, both for water and for fertile soil, which made growing crops easier. As communities grew, they became more complex. Leaders, called chieftains, looked after the well-being of people, and everyone worked together for the welfare of the community. The pictures of rock shelters and farming villages show men and women in set roles. Those roles may not always be accurate: women may also have painted on rocks and men may have cooked and cared for children. We have only limited information, so we should think carefully about them.

problem.en: Find how many years ago a person was born in 44 BCE, if the year now is 2024 CE.

text.en: Write the rule.

why.en: For a BCE date and a CE date, add them and subtract 1 because there is no year zero.

text.en: Add the numbers.
Subtract 1.

why.en: 2068 minus 1 is 2067, so the person was born 2067 years ago.

problem.en: Which century and millennium is the year 1500 CE in?

text.en: Count centuries from year 1 CE.

why.en: The 1st century is 1 to 100, so the 16th century is 1501 to 1600, and the 15th century is 1401 to 1500.

text.en: Place 1500.

why.en: 1500 is the last year of the 15th century.

text.en: Millennium.

why.en: The 2nd millennium CE is 1001 to 2000, so 1500 is in the 2nd millennium.

prompt.en: Explain how historians learn about the past and how early humans lived.

requiredIdeas.en: Historians use many kinds of sources such as oral, literary, archaeological, artistic and structures
Sources may match or disagree so historians decide which to trust
Experts such as archaeologists, epigraphists and scientists help
Early humans were hunters and gatherers who later began farming after the last Ice Age

commonMisconceptions.en: Thinking there is a year zero between BCE and CE
Thinking early humans already farmed 300000 years ago

points.en: History is the study of the human past; we learn from sources and measure time with calendars and timelines.
There is no year zero: add a BCE and a CE date and subtract 1 to find the gap.
A decade is 10 years, a century 100 years and a millennium 1000 years.
Sources include oral, literary, archaeological and artistic sources, structures, inscriptions and scientific studies.
Early humans hunted and gathered. After the last Ice Age, about 12000 years ago, they began to farm and settle near rivers.
